claim: IL6-mediated STAT3 signaling in hepatocytes, mediated via glycoprotein 130 (gp130; IL6ST), is generally accepted to be beneficial.
source: It is generally accepted that IL6-mediated STAT3 signaling in hepatocytes, mediated via glycoprotein 130 (gp130; IL6ST), is beneficial
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the abstract.

claim: The synthetic IL6:IL6ST fusion protein (HyperIL6) promotes liver regeneration.
source: It is generally accepted that IL6-mediated STAT3 signaling in hepatocytes, mediated via glycoprotein 130 (gp130; IL6ST), is beneficial and that the synthetic IL6:IL6ST fusion protein (HyperIL6) promotes liver regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the abstract.

claim: Autocrine IL11 activity acts via IL6ST but uses ERK rather than STAT3 to signal.
source: Recently, autocrine IL11 activity that also acts via IL6ST but uses ERK rather than STAT3 to signal, was found to be hepatotoxic.
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding in the abstract.

claim: Autocrine IL11 activity is hepatotoxic.
source: Recently, autocrine IL11 activity that also acts via IL6ST but uses ERK rather than STAT3 to signal, was found to be hepatotoxic.
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding in the abstract.

claim: HyperIL6 reduced N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (APAP)-induced cell death in human and mouse hepatocytes independent of STAT3 activation.
source: In human and mouse hepatocytes, HyperIL6 reduced N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (APAP)-induced cell death independent of STAT3 activation
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments described in the abstract.

claim: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11-related signaling and toxicities in human and mouse hepatocytes.
source: In human and mouse hepatocytes, HyperIL6 reduced N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (APAP)-induced cell death independent of STAT3 activation and instead, dose-dependently, inhibited IL11-related signaling and toxicities.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments described in the abstract.

claim: Expression of HyperIl6 reduced ERK activation in mice following administration of either IL11 or APAP.
source: In mice, expression of HyperIl6 reduced ERK activation and promoted STAT3-independent hepatic regeneration (PCNA, Cyclin D1, Ki67) following administration of either IL11 or APAP.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vivo experiments described in the abstract.

claim: Expression of HyperIl6 promoted STAT3-independent hepatic regeneration (PCNA, Cyclin D1, Ki67) in mice following administration of either IL11 or APAP.
source: In mice, expression of HyperIl6 reduced ERK activation and promoted STAT3-independent hepatic regeneration (PCNA, Cyclin D1, Ki67) following administration of either IL11 or APAP.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vivo experiments described in the abstract.

claim: Inhibition of putative intrinsic IL6 trans-signaling had no effect on liver regeneration in mice.
source: Inhibition of putative intrinsic IL6 trans-signaling had no effect on liver regeneration in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments described in the abstract.

claim: Mice deleted for Il11 exhibited spontaneous liver repair following APAP.
source: Following APAP, mice deleted for Il11 exhibited spontaneous liver repair
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments in Il11 knockout mice described in the abstract.

claim: HyperIl6 had no effect on liver regeneration in Il11 knockout mice despite robustly activating STAT3.
source: Following APAP, mice deleted for Il11 exhibited spontaneous liver repair but HyperIl6, despite robustly activating STAT3, had no effect on liver regeneration in this strain.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments in Il11 knockout mice described in the abstract.

claim: Synthetic IL6ST binding proteins such as HyperIL6 can have unexpected, on-target effects.
source: These data show that synthetic IL6ST binding proteins such as HyperIL6 can have unexpected, on-target effects
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the abstract.

claim: IL11, not IL6, is important for liver regeneration.
source: These data show that synthetic IL6ST binding proteins such as HyperIL6 can have unexpected, on-target effects and suggest IL11, not IL6, as important for liver regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the abstract.

claim: Replication of hepatocytes in midlobular zone two underlies liver regeneration.
source: Replication of hepatocytes in midlobular zone two underlies liver regeneration (Wei et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2021.

claim: A large number of cytokines and growth factors are implicated as mitogens in liver regeneration.
source: Replication of hepatocytes in midlobular zone two underlies liver regeneration (Wei et al., 2021), with a large number of cytokines and growth factors implicated as mitogens (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021.

claim: Interleukin 6 (IL6) binds with high affinity to its alpha receptor (IL6R) to signal in cis via glycoprotein 130 (gp130; IL6ST) and STAT3.
source: Interleukin 6 (IL6), a member of the larger IL6 family of cytokines, binds with high affinity to its alpha receptor (IL6R) to signal in cis via glycoprotein 130 (gp130; IL6ST) and STAT3.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about IL6 signaling.

claim: IL6 is believed to be a predominant auxiliary mitogen in liver regeneration.
source: Of all the cytokines implicated in liver regeneration, IL6 is believed to be a predominant auxiliary mitogen (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021; Schmidt-Arras and Rose-John, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021 and Schmidt-Arras and Rose-John, 2016.

claim: Mice globally deleted for Il6 exhibit reduced STAT3 activity and lesser liver regeneration following injury.
source: This belief is anchored on a seminal study performed in mice globally deleted for Il6, which exhibit reduced STAT3 activity and lesser liver regeneration following injury (Cressman et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cressman et al., 1996.

claim: IL6 can bind to a soluble form of its receptor (sIL6R) to signal in trans to activate IL6 signaling in cells that express IL6ST but low/or no IL6R.
source: It is thought that IL6 can bind to a soluble form of its receptor (sIL6R) to signal in trans to activate IL6 signaling in cells that express IL6ST but low/or no IL6R (Schmidt-Arras and Rose-John, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schmidt-Arras and Rose-John, 2016.

claim: HyperIL6 is an artificial fusion protein composed of a truncated form of human IL6R linked to human IL6.
source: This led to the design of an artificial fusion protein composed of a truncated form of human IL6R linked to human IL6 (HyperIL6).
evidence: This describes the composition of HyperIL6.

claim: HyperIL6 stimulates STAT3 signaling up to 1000-fold stronger than the respective separate molecules with high affinity for IL6ST.
source: HyperIL6 stimulates STAT3 signaling up to 1000-fold stronger than the respective separate molecules with high affinity for IL6ST (Fischer et al., 1997; Peters et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fischer et al., 1997 and Peters et al., 1998.

claim: The HyperIL6 superagonist can reverse fulminant liver failure due to toxin-induced liver damage.
source: The HyperIL6 superagonist can reverse fulminant liver failure due to toxin-induced liver damage (Galun et al., 2000; Hecht et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Galun et al., 2000 and Hecht et al., 2001.

claim: HyperIL6 can stimulate liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy.
source: The HyperIL6 superagonist can reverse fulminant liver failure due to toxin-induced liver damage (Galun et al., 2000; Hecht et al., 2001) and stimulate liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy (Peters et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peters et al., 2000.

claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the spinal cord.
source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leibinger et al., 2021.

claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the optic nerve.
source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021), optic nerve (Fischer, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fischer, 2017.

claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the kidney.
source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021), optic nerve (Fischer, 2017), kidney (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008.

claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the heart.
source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021), optic nerve (Fischer, 2017), kidney (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008), and heart (Matsushita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matsushita et al., 2005.

claim: IL11 is hepatotoxic and important for NASH pathologies.
source: We recently found that IL11, a little studied IL6 family protein, is hepatotoxic and important for NASH pathologies (Dong et al., 2021; Widjaja et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2021 and Widjaja et al., 2019.

claim: In APAP-induced liver injury, IL11 activates NOX4, ERK and JNK and impedes liver regeneration.
source: Furthermore, in a recent study of N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (APAP)-induced liver injury, IL11 was shown to activate NOX4, ERK and JNK and impede liver regeneration (Widjaja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Widjaja et al., 2021.

claim: Synthetic, IL6ST-binding proteins can compete with endogenous IL11 for binding to IL6ST and reduce APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
source: Interestingly, this study demonstrated that synthetic, IL6ST-binding proteins can compete with endogenous IL11 for binding to IL6ST and reduce APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by reference to a recent study (Widjaja et al., 2021).

claim: APAP poisoning is a common cause of liver damage, associated with impaired liver regeneration.
source: APAP poisoning is a common cause of liver damage, associated with impaired liver regeneration (Bernal and Wendon, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bernal and Wendon, 2013.

claim: In primary human hepatocytes cultures, incubation with APAP for 24 hr caused cell death in approximately 40% of cells.
source: In primary human hepatocytes cultures, incubation with APAP for 24 hr caused cell death in approximately 40% of cells (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Inhibition of IL11 signaling using a neutralizing IL11RA antibody (X209) reduced ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity and cell death in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
source: Inhibition of IL11 signaling using a neutralizing IL11RA antibody (X209) reduced ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity and cell death (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C.

claim: Antibody-based neutralization of IL6ST reduced ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity and cell death in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
source: These phenotypes were mirrored by antibody-based neutralization of IL6ST.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1A–C.

claim: HyperIL6 inhibited APAP-induced cell death in hepatocytes, which was associated with increased STAT3 phosphorylation and lesser ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity.
source: HyperIL6 also inhibited APAP-induced cell death, and this was associated with increased STAT3 phosphorylation and lesser ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: In human hepatocytes, HyperIL6 markedly induced STAT3 phosphorylation but had minimal effect on ERK and no effect on AKT.
source: In human hepatocytes, HyperIL6 markedly induced STAT3 phosphorylation but had minimal effect on ERK and no effect on AKT (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inhibition of IL11 signaling with X209 or anti-IL6ST reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels.
source: Inhibition of IL11 signaling with X209 or anti-IL6ST reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels, which was also true for HyperIL6 (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HyperIL6 reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels.
source: Inhibition of IL11 signaling with X209 or anti-IL6ST reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels, which was also true for HyperIL6 (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S3I-201 (a STAT3 inhibitor) had no effect on the protection afforded by HyperIL6 in hepatocytes exposed to APAP despite inhibiting STAT3 activation.
source: Interestingly, S3I-201 (a STAT3 inhibitor; iSTAT3) had no effect on the protection afforded by HyperIL6 despite inhibiting STAT3 activation (Figure 1A, F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, F and G.

claim: S3I-201 had no effect on HyperIL6-induced cell death, ROS induction, or GSH depletion in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
source: Furthermore, S3I-201 had no effect on HyperIL6-induced cell death, ROS induction, or GSH depletion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1A–C and E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: S3I-201 inhibited STAT3 activation, but not ERK or JNK phosphorylation nor NOX4 upregulation in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
source: At the signaling level, S3I-201 inhibited STAT3 activation, but not ERK or JNK phosphorylation nor NOX4 upregulation (Figure 1A–C and E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C and E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The beneficial effects of HyperIL6 are unrelated to STAT3 activity but instead reflect competitive inhibition of IL11 signaling.
source: These experiments suggest that the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 are unrelated to STAT3 activity but instead reflect competitive inhibition of IL11 signaling (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Incubation of hepatocytes with IL11 resulted in ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activation and cell death.
source: Incubation of hepatocytes with IL11 resulted in ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activation and cell death, as expected and similar to that seen with APAP (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F; Widjaja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F and citation to Widjaja et al., 2021.

claim: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11 signaling and toxicity in hepatocytes independent of STAT3 phosphorylation.
source: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11 signaling and toxicity that was independent of STAT3 phosphorylation and could be titrated away by the addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST) (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The inhibitory effects of HyperIL6 on IL11 signaling and toxicity could be titrated away by the addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST).
source: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11 signaling and toxicity that was independent of STAT3 phosphorylation and could be titrated away by the addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST) (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity in human hepatocytes could be dose-dependently inhibited by the addition of sIL6ST.
source: We went on to show that the protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity in human hepatocytes could be dose-dependently inhibited by the addition of sIL6ST.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: The protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity were STAT3 independent and instead related to inhibition of IL11 signaling.
source: We confirmed again that the protective effects of HyperIL6 were STAT3 independent and instead related to inhibition of IL11 signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a dissociation constant (KD) of 1 nM.
source: In binding assays, HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a similar dissociation constant as an IL11:IL11RA construct (HyperIL11) (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: HyperIL11 bound to IL6ST with a dissociation constant (KD) of 0.95 nM.
source: In binding assays, HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a similar dissociation constant as an IL11:IL11RA construct (HyperIL11) (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: IL6 alone did not bind to IL6ST.
source: In binding assays, HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a similar dissociation constant as an IL11:IL11RA construct (HyperIL11) (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively), whereas IL6 alone did not bind to IL6ST (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The binding data would be consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6.
source: These data would be consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding assay data.

claim: The competitive inhibition of IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by HyperIL6 may explain why IL6 alone is ineffective for liver regeneration.
source: These data would be consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6 and may explain why IL6 alone is ineffective for liver regeneration (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding assay data and supported by citation to Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011.

claim: Both recombinant mouse HyperIL6 (rm-HyperIL6) and recombinant human HyperIL6 (rh-HyperIL6) equally reduced serum ALT and AST levels in the mouse model of APAP injury.
source: We found that both constructs equally reduced serum (alanine transaminase) ALT and (aspartate aminotransferase) AST levels and GSH depletion (Figure 2B–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claim: Both rm-HyperIL6 and rh-HyperIL6 equally reduced GSH depletion in the mouse model of APAP injury.
source: We found that both constructs equally reduced serum (alanine transaminase) ALT and (aspartate aminotransferase) AST levels and GSH depletion (Figure 2B–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claim: Both rm-HyperIL6 and rh-HyperIL6 activated STAT3 and inhibited ERK and JNK phosphorylation in the mouse model of APAP injury.
source: We found that both constructs equally reduced serum (alanine transaminase) ALT and (aspartate aminotransferase) AST levels and GSH depletion (Figure 2B–D), activated STAT3, and inhibited ERK and JNK phosphorylation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both rm-HyperIL6 and rh-HyperIL6 reduced centrilobular necrosis in the mouse model of APAP injury.
source: Histology showed both constructs also reduced centrilobular necrosis, pathognomonic of APAP liver damage (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mice over-expressing HyperIL6 had lower ALT/AST levels 24 hr after APAP as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group.
source: The day after APAP (24 hr), mice over-expressing HyperIL6 (Figure 2H) or receiving an anti-IL11RA antibody (X209) had lower ALT/AST levels as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I,J.

claim: Mice receiving an anti-IL11RA antibody (X209) had lower ALT/AST levels 24 hr after APAP as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group.
source: The day after APAP (24 hr), mice over-expressing HyperIL6 (Figure 2H) or receiving an anti-IL11RA antibody (X209) had lower ALT/AST levels as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I,J.

claim: AAV8-Alb-sIl6st had no effect on APAP-induced liver injury despite inducing high sIL6ST expression.
source: While AAV8-Alb-sIl6st induced high sIL6ST expression, it had no effect on APAP-induced liver injury (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I–K.

claim: Liver regeneration is associated with a signature of increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression.
source: Liver regeneration is associated with a signature of increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Sekiya and Suzuki, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sekiya and Suzuki, 2011.

claim: Increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression was apparent 24 hr post-APAP in both HyperIL6-expressing mice and X209-treated mice but not in AAV8-Alb-Null+ IgG or in sIl6st-expressing mice.
source: Liver regeneration is associated with a signature of increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Sekiya and Suzuki, 2011), which was apparent 24 hr post-APAP in both HyperIL6-expressing mice and X209-treated mice but not in AAV8-Alb-Null+ IgG or in sIl6st-expressing mice (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels following APAP.
source: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels and inhibited ERK and JNK activation, whereas STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice (Figure 2L,M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L,M.

claim: HyperIL6 or X209 inhibited ERK and JNK activation following APAP.
source: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels and inhibited ERK and JNK activation, whereas STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice (Figure 2L,M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L,M.

claim: STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice following APAP.
source: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels and inhibited ERK and JNK activation, whereas STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice (Figure 2L,M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L,M.

claim: Histology revealed typical centrilobular necrosis in APAP-treated AAV8-Alb-Null or sIl6st expressing mice, which was lesser in mice expressing HyperIL6 or following X209 administration.
source: Histology revealed typical centrilobular necrosis in APAP-treated AAV8-Alb-Null or sIl6st expressing mice, which was lesser in mice expressing HyperIL6 or following X209 administration (Figure 2N).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: Both human and mouse HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice.
source: These data show that both human and mouse HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Inhibition of IL11 signaling, not activation of STAT3, likely underlies HyperIL6 effects on APAP-induced liver damage.
source: These data show that both human and mouse HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice and show that inhibition of IL11 signaling, not activation of STAT3, likely underlies HyperIL6 effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The data rule out a pro-regenerative effect of putative endogenous trans-IL6 signaling.
source: The data also rule out a pro-regenerative effect of putative endogenous trans-IL6 signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels.
source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had improved hepatic GSH levels.
source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had lesser ERK/JNK activity.
source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had diminished centrilobular necrosis.
source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Elevated STAT3 phosphorylation was observed in APAP-treated control mice that was further increased in AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6 mice but absent in mice receiving S3I-201.
source: We observed elevated STAT3 phosphorylation in APAP-treated control mice that was further increased in AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6 mice but absent in mice receiving S3I-201 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection are STAT3 independent at 6 hr post-APAP.
source: Thus, the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection are STAT3 independent at this early time point of assessment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Markers of liver regeneration peak some 48 hr following liver injury.
source: Markers of liver regeneration peak some 48 hr following liver injury (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021.

claim: APAP liver toxicities can be affected by the administration of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).
source: In addition, APAP liver toxicities can be affected by the administration of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), which we used for S31-201 stock solutions (Park et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Park et al., 1988.

claim: Two days (48 hr) after APAP dosing, APAP and APAP+ DMSO treatment groups were indistinguishable with equally elevated ALT/AST, reduced GSH, activated ERK/JNK, diminished PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, and similar patterns of centrilobular necrosis.
source: Two days (48 hr) after APAP dosing, APAP and APAP+ DMSO treatment groups were indistinguishable with equally elevated ALT/AST, reduced GSH, activated ERK/JNK, diminished PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, and similar patterns of centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 were equally protected from liver damage with lower ALT/AST, higher GSH, and greater expression of PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, while having reduced centrilobular necrosis at 48 hr post-APAP.
source: Mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 were equally protected from liver damage with lower ALT/AST, higher GSH, and greater expression of PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, while having reduced centrilobular necrosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 48 hr post-APAP, mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 had similarly reduced ERK and JNK signaling.
source: At the signaling level, mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 had similarly reduced ERK and JNK signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only mice with HyperIL6 alone had increased STAT3 phosphorylation at 48 hr post-APAP that was unrelated to the phenotypes studied.
source: Only mice with HyperIL6 alone had increased STAT3 phosphorylation that was unrelated to the phenotypes studied here (Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection and regeneration are STAT3 independent at 48 hr post-APAP.
source: Thus the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection and regeneration are STAT3 independent at this later time point of assessment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Injection of recombinant mouse IL11 (rmIL11) to mice (6 hr) resulted in elevated ALT/AST levels and activation of ERK and JNK.
source: Injection of rmIL11 to mice (6 hr) resulted in elevated ALT/AST levels and activation of ERK and JNK, as expected (Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Widjaja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and citation to Widjaja et al., 2021.

claim: Following rmIL11 injection, mice expressing HyperIL6 had elevated STAT3 phosphorylation, lower ALT/AST levels and lesser activation of ERK and JNK, as compared to controls.
source: Following rmIL11 injection, mice expressing HyperIL6 had elevated STAT3 phosphorylation, lower ALT/AST levels and lesser activation of ERK and JNK, as compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Administration of S3I-201 to HyperIL6 expressing mice reduced STAT3 activity to baseline but had no effect on its beneficial outcomes following rmIL11 injection.
source: Administration of S3I-201 to HyperIL6 expressing mice reduced STAT3 activity to baseline but had no effect on its beneficial outcomes at any level of assessment. (Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: If the protective effects of HyperIL6 are due to its inhibition of IL11 signaling, then HyperIL6 should be ineffective in APAP injury in the absence of IL11.
source: If the protective effects of HyperIL6 are due to its inhibition of IL11 signaling, then HyperIL6 should be ineffective in APAP injury in the absence of IL11.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: APAP dosing resulted in increased IL11 expression in the injured livers of wild-type (WT) mice that was absent in Il11−/− mice.
source: APAP dosing resulted in increased IL11 expression in the injured livers of wild-type (WT) mice that was, as expected, absent in Il11−/− mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Following APAP, expression of HyperIL6 in WT mice was associated with lesser liver damage and a molecular signature of regeneration as compared to WT controls.
source: Following APAP, as compared to WT controls, expression of HyperIL6 in WT mice was associated with lesser liver damage and a molecular signature of regeneration (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–F.

claim: As compared to WT mice receiving APAP, Il11−/− mice dosed with APAP had reduced ALT, AST, and centrilobular necrosis, higher GSH levels along with increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression.
source: As compared to WT mice receiving APAP, Il11−/− mice dosed with APAP had reduced ALT, AST, and centrilobular necrosis, higher GSH levels along with increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lack of IL11 signaling due to genetic deletion of Il11 stimulates regeneration following APAP.
source: Thus lack of IL11 signaling due to genetic deletion if Il11 stimulates regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Il11 knockout mice.

claim: Expression of HyperIL6 had no additive effect on hepatoprotection or liver regeneration in Il11−/− mice.
source: Notably, expression of HyperIL6 had no additive effect on hepatoprotection or liver regeneration in Il11−/− mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: APAP-related ERK and JNK activation were reduced in both HyperIL6-expressing WT mice and in Il11−/− mice in the absence of HyperIL6.
source: At the signaling level, APAP-related ERK and JNK activation were reduced in both HyperIL6-expressing WT mice and in Il11−/− mice in the absence of HyperIL6 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: While HyperIL6 expression robustly increased STAT3 phosphorylation in both WT and Il11−/− mice, this activity was unrelated to liver protection or regeneration.
source: While HyperIL6 expression robustly increased STAT3 phosphorylation in both WT and Il11−/− mice, this activity was unrelated to liver protection or regeneration (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–G.

claim: HyperIL6-mediated inhibition of IL11 signaling (NOX4, ERK, and JNK) in APAP-injured hepatocytes is the dominant mechanism underlying the pro-regenerative effects of HyperIL6 in the damaged liver.
source: Here we show that HyperIL6-mediated inhibition of IL11 signaling (NOX4, ERK, and JNK; Widjaja et al., 2021; Widjaja et al., 2020) in APAP-injured hepatocytes, latent until now, is the dominant mechanism underlying the pro-regenerative effects of HyperIL6 in the damaged liver.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data and citations to Widjaja et al., 2021 and Widjaja et al., 2020.

claim: Competition of HyperIL6 with IL11:IL11RA complexes for binding to IL6ST could explain why injection of HyperIL6, but not IL6 itself, promotes liver regeneration.
source: We postulate that competition of HyperIL6 with IL11:IL11RA complexes for binding to IL6ST could explain why injection of HyperIL6, but not IL6 itself, promotes liver regeneration (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a postulate based on the study findings and supported by citation to Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011.

claim: Caution is needed when interpreting assumed gain-of-function, on-target effects of synthetic IL6ST-interacting molecules such as HyperIL6, NT-3N or IC7Fc fusion molecule.
source: Our study suggests that caution is needed when interpreting assumed gain-of-function, on-target effects of synthetic IL6ST-interacting molecules such as HyperIL6, NT-3N (Nishina et al., 2012) or the recently described IC7Fc fusion molecule (Findeisen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings and supported by citations to Nishina et al., 2012 and Findeisen et al., 2019.

claim: IL6ST-related ligand, interacting alpha receptor, and signaling pleiotropy is large, and mechanism of effect is hard to decipher using overexpression of synthetic and alien factors.
source: IL6ST-related ligand, interacting alpha receptor, and signaling pleiotropy is large, and mechanism of effect is hard to decipher using overexpression of synthetic and alien factors.
evidence: This is a general statement about the complexity of IL6ST signaling.

claim: IL11 instead of IL6 should be the focus for regenerative studies of the liver and perhaps nerves and kidney.
source: We end by suggesting IL11 instead of IL6 as a focus for regenerative studies of the liver and perhaps nerves (Fischer, 2017; Leibinger et al., 2021) and kidney (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the study findings and supported by citations to Fischer, 2017; Leibinger et al., 2021; and Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008.

claim: Anti-IL11 therapies are advancing toward the clinic.
source: With anti-IL11 therapies advancing toward the clinic, this provides interesting opportunities.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the current state of anti-IL11 therapy development.

claim: Human IL6 and IL6R have limited conservation with mouse orthologs (41% and 53.4%, respectively).
source: This could have unappreciated off-target effects, toxicities, and/or immunogenicity issues as human IL6 and IL6R have limited conservation with mouse orthologs (41% and 53.4%, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the sequence conservation between human and mouse IL6 and IL6R.
